554.title: Viradha
554.hook: the giant falls, and at the edge of a freshly dug pit he suddenly remembers who he used to be
554.howItsDone: Hindu storytellers often point to Viradha as the first of several beings in the Ramayana released from a curse by meeting Rama, a pattern many devotees read as a sign of his grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Viradha, the giant no weapon can kill. He seized Sita and carried off the brothers, until they broke his arms.

Here's the problem. Viradha is down, arms broken, but no weapon can kill him. Brahma's boon still holds. So what do you do with an enemy who can't die the ordinary way? Rama tells Lakshmana to dig a pit, a deep one, big enough for a body that size. While Lakshmana digs, Rama puts his foot on Viradha's throat to hold him down. That's when the giant's face changes.
screen: `AN ENEMY WHO CAN'T DIE.` → `DIG A PIT.` → `THE GIANT'S FACE CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Viradha looks up and recognizes him. You're Rama, Kausalya's son. I was told you would come. Then he tells his story. He wasn't always a forest giant. He was a gandharva, one of the celestial musicians, named Tumburu, who served Kubera, the lord of wealth. But he fell in love with Rambha, one of the apsaras, and in his longing he neglected his duty and didn't show up when he should have. Kubera cursed him: become a rakshasa, a terror of the forest. Tumburu begged for mercy, and Kubera set a limit. When Rama, son of Dasharatha, kills you in battle, you'll be released and return to heaven. So through all those years of being monstrous, Viradha was waiting for this. He even tells them how to finish it. Bury me; it's the way for one like me. And one more thing: a few miles from here lives a great sage, Sharabhanga. Go to him. He'll help you. So the brothers lower him into the pit, and as the earth covers him, Viradha leaves the body and rises, released. Yesterday he was the forest's first monster. Today he's a cursed musician who was waiting to be set free. The Ramayana does this again and again: under a terrifying face, a story, a curse and a release. The enemy becomes the guide who points the way.
screen: `YOU'RE RAMA. I WAS TOLD YOU'D COME.` · `TUMBURU, A CURSED MUSICIAN.` · `BURY ME. GO TO SHARABHANGA.` · `RISING, RELEASED.` · then, large: `THE ENEMY BECOMES THE GUIDE.`

555.title: Sharabhanga
555.hook: a king of the gods is visiting an old sage, and when Rama walks up, the god leaves
555.howItsDone: In the text, Indra withdraws before meeting Rama, and some devotees read the scene as the gods waiting on Rama's mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the enemy becomes the guide. Viradha rose free from the pit, a cursed musician released, and sent the brothers to a sage.

Rama follows Viradha's directions, and near Sharabhanga's hermitage he stops. There's a chariot in the air above the clearing, blazing like the sun, pulled by green horses. A white umbrella shades the figure in it, and attendants crowd around. That's Indra, Rama tells Lakshmana, king of the gods, talking with the sage. And as the brothers walk closer, Indra says something to his companions, and the chariot rises and goes.
screen: `A CHARIOT ABOVE THE CLEARING.` → `INDRA, KING OF THE GODS.` → `HE LEAVES AS RAMA COMES.`

segments.voice: Why does Indra leave? Valmiki gives a reason, spoken to the people around him. Rama is coming, and I shouldn't meet him yet. He has work to do first. When it's done, I'll see him. The text hints at what lies ahead, a war the gods themselves need Rama to fight, but says no more. The point is the picture: the god of storms and rain stepping aside for a man in bark clothes. Rama goes in, and the very old sage welcomes him. Indra came to take me to Brahma's world, Sharabhanga says. I've earned it by my austerities. But I heard you were near, and I wouldn't leave until I had seen my guest. Then the old sage makes an extraordinary offer. All the worlds I've won by my tapas, all that merit, I give to you. Take it. Rama says no, kindly. I'll earn my own worlds. Just tell me where in this forest I should live. A free gift of heaven, from someone who means it, and Rama turns it down, not out of pride but because he has his own road to walk. Sharabhanga accepts that, and points him to Sutikshna, another sage further on. But first he asks Rama to stay a little longer and watch. He has one last thing to do.

556.title: Sharabhanga
556.hook: an old man lights a fire and steps into it, and then the other sages show Rama what they've been hiding
556.howItsDone: Ramayana reciters tell Sharabhanga's departure with reverence, and Rama's promise to the sages here sets up the battles later in the Aranya Kanda.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, I'll earn my own worlds. Sharabhanga offered Rama all his merit, and Rama kindly said no.

Sharabhanga asks Rama to wait and watch. He builds a fire, makes the offering of clarified butter, and with the words of the rite, steps into the flames. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana stand there. The old body burns away. And out of the fire, Valmiki says, rises a young man, shining, who goes up to the world of Brahma. The sage had waited only for this: to see his guest, and then to go.
screen: `WAIT AND WATCH.` → `HE STEPS INTO THE FIRE.` → `A YOUNG MAN RISES.`

segments.voice: It's important to say what this scene is and isn't. Sharabhanga is a great ascetic at the very end of a long life of tapas, already invited to heaven by Indra himself. His entry into the fire is presented as a sacred departure, a completed life, not a despairing one, and the text treats it with awe. Then the mood changes. Word has spread that Rama is here, and the sages gather around him, many kinds of ascetics, Valmiki says, some living on water alone, some on air, some standing in rivers. They lead him to a place in the forest where bones are piled up: the bodies of sages killed by rakshasas, the man-eating demons who roam Dandaka. Look, they say. This is what happens to us. They're slaughtering us, and we have no protector. You are our refuge. Remember the sages' first request: be our king, protect us. Now Rama sees why. Not a vague danger, but this. And he answers directly. I came to this forest to keep my father's word, but I'll do this too. I'll destroy the rakshasas who harm you. That promise matters. It's freely made, by a man under no orders, in front of witnesses. And in the chapters ahead it will be tested, and questioned, by someone very close to him.
screen: `A SACRED DEPARTURE, NOT DESPAIR.` · `THE SAGES GATHER.` · `A PILE OF BONES IN THE FOREST.` · `RAMA'S PROMISE.` · then, large: `I'LL PROTECT YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've seen recently that wasn't right, something real, not abstract, and look at it honestly for a moment, the way Rama looked at what the sages showed him, without flooding yourself. 557.title: Agastya's weapons
557.hook: before a great sage hands Rama new weapons, Sita asks whether he should be carrying weapons at all
557.carry: fire is kindled by being near fuel
557.howItsDone: Reciters give Sita's question about weapons in the Aranya Kanda its full length, and Hindu teachers who discuss it note that the text lets both her concern and Rama's answer stand.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, I'll protect you. The sages showed Rama the bones, and he promised to stand between them and the rakshasas.

They're walking between hermitages, Rama ahead with his bow, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind. The path is narrow, the trees close, and nobody has spoken for a while. Then Sita, quietly, starts to talk. She's been thinking about that promise. She doesn't doubt Rama's goodness. She's worried about something else. You vowed to kill the rakshasas, and they haven't done anything to you. I'm afraid of what weapons do to the person who carries them.
screen: `SITA STARTS TO TALK.` → `THEY'VE DONE NOTHING TO YOU.` → `WHAT WEAPONS DO TO THEIR BEARER.`

segments.voice: She lays out her worry carefully. Three faults come from desire, she says: speaking falsely, wanting someone else's wife, and violence without enmity, harming those who haven't harmed you. You've never done the first two. The third worries me. Then she tells a story. Once there was an ascetic so devoted that Indra, king of the gods, grew uneasy. So Indra came disguised as a warrior and left a sword with him for safekeeping. The ascetic took the trust seriously and carried the sword everywhere: to gather fruit, to bathe, to pray. Slowly, without noticing, he grew rough, then cruel, and lost his practice. Fire, she says, is kindled by being near fuel. Here in the forest, let's live the forest's way; at home in Ayodhya you can take up a warrior's duty again. I only say this out of love. Rama's answer is just as tender. You say this because you care for me. But a warrior carries a bow so no one in distress cries out unheard. The sages came to me for refuge, and I gave my word. I could give up my life, even you, even Lakshmana, sooner than a promise made to them. Two good people, two real concerns, and the text lets both speak. Then ten years pass, the text says, in the hermitages of Dandaka, and the road leads to the sage Rama has been told to seek: Agastya.
screen: `THREE FAULTS FROM DESIRE.` · `THE ASCETIC AND THE SWORD.` · `I SAY THIS OUT OF LOVE.` · `NO ONE CRIES OUT UNHEARD.` · then, large: `TWO GOOD PEOPLE, BOTH HEARD.`

558.title: Agastya's weapons
558.hook: the sage who once ate a demon for lunch hands Rama a bow that belonged to a god
558.carry: they come with a blessing, not a grudge
558.howItsDone: Agastya is honored in tradition as the great sage of the south, and the story of Vatapi and Ilvala is a familiar one in Hindu storytelling, for children and adults alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fire is kindled by being near fuel. Sita asked whether carrying weapons would change Rama, and he answered with his promise.

On the way to Agastya, Rama tells Lakshmana a story about him, the kind people tell about a legend before you meet one. Two demon brothers, Ilvala and Vatapi, used to trap holy men. Ilvala would turn Vatapi into a ram, cook him, and serve him to a guest. Then he'd call his brother's name, and Vatapi would burst out of the guest's body, killing him. It worked many times. Until they served the meal to Agastya.
screen: `ILVALA AND VATAPI.` → `A RAM SERVED TO GUESTS.` → `UNTIL THEY FED AGASTYA.`

segments.voice: Agastya ate the meal. Ilvala called: Vatapi, come out. Nothing happened. Agastya, the story goes, had simply digested him. When Ilvala attacked in fury, the sage burned him with a look. Since then, Rama says, the southern country has been safe for sages, and even the rakshasas only look at it from a distance. So Agastya's hermitage, with shrines to the gods all around, is a place of real power. The old sage welcomes them warmly with water and food, and then, unasked, gives Rama weapons. A great bow adorned with gold and gems, made by Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods, and once Vishnu's. An arrow from Brahma that never misses. Two quivers from Indra that never run out of arrows. And a sword in a golden sheath. Remember Sita's worry: what weapons do to the person who carries them. One way to read this scene: these weapons come from a sage, a man of tapas, given freely and unasked, for the protection of others. They come with a blessing, not a grudge. Then Agastya gives one more gift: advice. Nearby, by the Godavari river, is a beautiful place full of fruit, flowers and water, called Panchavati. Live there, and protect the sages from there.

559.title: Panchavati
559.hook: on the road to a new home, a giant bird lands in front of them and says he knew their father
559.carry: a brother builds a house with his hands
559.howItsDone: Panchavati is identified by many pilgrims with a site at Nashik on the Godavari, and the hut Lakshmana builds is a favorite scene in Ramayana art and performance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Agastya's weapons. The sage who digested a demon gave Rama Vishnu's bow and sent him on to Panchavati: they come with a blessing, not a grudge.

Halfway there, a huge bird settles on a tree in front of them. A vulture, enormous and old. After Viradha, Rama's first thought is a rakshasa in disguise, and he asks who it is. The bird answers gently. I was a friend of your father, he says. My name is Jatayu. And he offers what no one else has: when you two brothers go out into the forest, I'll stay and watch over Sita.
screen: `A GIANT BIRD ON A TREE.` → `I WAS YOUR FATHER'S FRIEND.` → `I'LL WATCH OVER SITA.`

segments.voice: Jatayu, the vulture king, gives his lineage, a long one reaching back to the beginning of creatures. Hearing that he was Dasharatha's friend, Rama embraces him. It's a brief meeting, but hold on to it: of everyone in the forest book, this old bird's promise to guard Sita will cost the most. Then they reach Panchavati, usually explained as the place of five banyan trees. It sits on the Godavari, with flowering trees, deer, peacocks, and mountains in the distance. Rama turns to Lakshmana: you choose the spot. Lakshmana would rather be told. As long as you live, he says, I'm here to do what you ask. So Rama picks a level place near the water, and Lakshmana builds the hut. Valmiki describes it with pleasure: walls of packed earth, posts of bamboo, a roof of leaves and long grass, a floor made smooth. Then Lakshmana bathes in the river, gathers flowers and fruit, and makes an offering for the new home. Rama is moved. He holds his brother and says something close to this: with you here, it's as if our father is not gone. That's the heart of Panchavati. Not the scenery, lovely as it is, but a brother building a house with his own hands so the family has a place to live again.

560.title: Panchavati
560.hook: a cold winter dawn by the river, and a brother says one sentence too many
560.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers cite Rama's refusal to let Lakshmana speak ill of Kaikeyi as an example of restraint in speech within a family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jatayu promised to guard Sita, and Lakshmana built the hut by the Godavari. A brother builds a house with his hands.

Time passes at Panchavati, and the season turns to hemanta, early winter. One morning before sunrise, the three of them walk down to the Godavari to bathe. Lakshmana carries the water pot, and he talks, the way people do on cold walks. Mist over the fields. The sun weak and far away. Water so cold, he says, that even the elephants touch it with their trunks and pull back.
screen: `HEMANTA: THE COLD SEASON.` → `A WALK TO THE RIVER AT DAWN.` → `EVEN THE ELEPHANTS PULL BACK.`

segments.voice: Then Lakshmana's mind goes home. Right now, he says, Bharata is probably walking down to the Sarayu in this same cold. He could be living in a palace. Instead he sleeps on the ground and keeps an ascetic's vows, out of love for you. Then he adds one sentence too many. How could a mother like Kaikeyi have a son like Bharata? Rama stops him. Don't speak badly of our middle mother, he says. Speak only of Bharata. And he says how much he misses him: Bharata's kind words, Rama says, come back to him like nectar. He longs to see him, and Shatrughna, and all of them. Rama lost a kingdom to Kaikeyi's wish, and he's the one who won't allow the bitterness. He doesn't argue that she was right. He just won't let the talk turn sour. Now the week. Viradha, the giant who was a cursed musician. Sharabhanga, who waited to see Rama before going to heaven, and the bones that brought Rama's promise. Sita's question about weapons, and Rama's answer. Agastya, who digested a demon and gave Rama a god's bow. Jatayu's offer to guard Sita. And Panchavati: a hut, a brother's handiwork, and a cold morning where blame is stopped at the door. This quiet is about to end.
screen: `BHARATA IN THE SAME COLD.` · `HOW COULD SHE HAVE SUCH A SON?` · `SPEAK ONLY OF BHARATA.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `BLAME STOPPED AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Feel the breath come in a little cool through the nose and leave warm. Think of someone you've been tempted to complain about, then bring to mind someone connected to them whom you love or admire. Rest your attention on the good one, breathing in cool and out warm.
